claim: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the leading monogenic cause of intellectual disability and autism.
source: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the leading monogenic cause of intellectual disability and autism. This disorder arises from mutations in the Fmr1 gene resulting in a loss of fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) (Salcedo-Arellano et al., 2020; Willemsen and Kooy, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Salcedo-Arellano et al., 2020; Willemsen and Kooy, 2017).

claim: FXS arises from mutations in the Fmr1 gene resulting in a loss of FMRP.
source: This disorder arises from mutations in the Fmr1 gene resulting in a loss of fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) (Salcedo-Arellano et al., 2020; Willemsen and Kooy, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Salcedo-Arellano et al., 2020; Willemsen and Kooy, 2017).

claim: Hippocampus is one of the most affected brain regions in FXS.
source: Hippocampus, the brain area implicated as a central hub for learning and memory, is one of the most affected brain regions in FXS (Bostrom et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Bostrom et al., 2016).

claim: Dentate gyrus receives the bulk of cortical inputs within the hippocampus.
source: Within the hippocampus, dentate gyrus receives the bulk of cortical inputs and plays a critical role in many core information processing functions (Amaral et al., 2007), which are often dysregulated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including FXS (Deng et al., 2022; Eadie et al., 2012; Ghilan et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2020; Yau et al., 2018; Yau et al., 2016; Yun and Trommer, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Amaral et al., 2007).

claim: Dentate gyrus plays a critical role in many core information processing functions.
source: Within the hippocampus, dentate gyrus receives the bulk of cortical inputs and plays a critical role in many core information processing functions (Amaral et al., 2007), which are often dysregulated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including FXS (Deng et al., 2022; Eadie et al., 2012; Ghilan et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2020; Yau et al., 2018; Yau et al., 2016; Yun and Trommer, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Amaral et al., 2007).

claim: Dentate gyrus information processing functions are often dysregulated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including FXS.
source: Within the hippocampus, dentate gyrus receives the bulk of cortical inputs and plays a critical role in many core information processing functions (Amaral et al., 2007), which are often dysregulated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including FXS (Deng et al., 2022; Eadie et al., 2012; Ghilan et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2020; Yau et al., 2018; Yau et al., 2016; Yun and Trommer, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Deng et al., 2022; Eadie et al., 2012; Ghilan et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2020; Yau et al., 2018; Yau et al., 2016; Yun and Trommer, 2011).

claim: Dentate gyrus has two types of glutamatergic excitatory neurons: granule cells and mossy cells.
source: Distinct from other hippocampal regions, dentate gyrus has two types of glutamatergic excitatory neurons (Figure 1A): granule cells and mossy cells (MCs) (Amaral et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Amaral et al., 2007) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Granule cells are the first-station neurons of canonical trisynaptic pathway and the only type of output cells in the dentate gyrus.
source: Granule cells are the first-station neurons of canonical trisynaptic pathway and the only type of output cells in the dentate gyrus (Amaral et al., 2007), whereas MCs comprise a significant portion of neurons in the hilus region (Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018), which is sandwiched between the two blades of the granule cell layer.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Amaral et al., 2007).

claim: Mossy cells comprise a significant portion of neurons in the hilus region.
source: Granule cells are the first-station neurons of canonical trisynaptic pathway and the only type of output cells in the dentate gyrus (Amaral et al., 2007), whereas MCs comprise a significant portion of neurons in the hilus region (Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018), which is sandwiched between the two blades of the granule cell layer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018).

claim: Mossy cells can directly excite granule cells.
source: MCs are in a unique position to control dentate gyrus output because these cells not only can directly excite granule cells, but also indirectly inhibit them through innervating local GABAergic interneurons (Amaral et al., 2007), which play a central role in controlling granule cell activity (Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Amaral et al., 2007).

claim: Mossy cells can indirectly inhibit granule cells through innervating local GABAergic interneurons.
source: MCs are in a unique position to control dentate gyrus output because these cells not only can directly excite granule cells, but also indirectly inhibit them through innervating local GABAergic interneurons (Amaral et al., 2007), which play a central role in controlling granule cell activity (Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Amaral et al., 2007).

claim: Local GABAergic interneurons play a central role in controlling granule cell activity.
source: MCs are in a unique position to control dentate gyrus output because these cells not only can directly excite granule cells, but also indirectly inhibit them through innervating local GABAergic interneurons (Amaral et al., 2007), which play a central role in controlling granule cell activity (Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Pelkey et al., 2017).

claim: Both mossy cells and hilar interneurons have been implicated in various pathological conditions.
source: Both MCs and hilar interneurons have been implicated in various pathological conditions (Pelkey et al., 2017; Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018; Noebels et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pelkey et al., 2017; Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018; Noebels et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of FMRP markedly decreased excitability of dentate mossy cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that loss of FMRP significantly decreased excitability of MCs, as evident by the reduced number of APs fired (Figure 1B and C; statistical data for every measurement in this study are listed in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Mossy cell hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice is opposite to all other known excitability defects in excitatory neurons in FXS.
source: This hypo-excitability is opposite to the changes previously observed in other excitatory neurons in FXS models, which typically exhibit hyperexcitability (Contractor et al., 2015; Deng and Klyachko, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Contractor et al., 2015; Deng and Klyachko, 2021).

claim: Loss of FMRP increased voltage threshold in mossy cells.
source: Similarly, we found a decreased number of APs fired (Figure 1D and E), as well as increased voltage threshold, rheobase, and rheobase charge transfer in MCs of Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 1D and F–H), confirming the hypo-excitable state of MCs in the absence of FMRP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: Loss of FMRP increased rheobase in mossy cells.
source: Similarly, we found a decreased number of APs fired (Figure 1D and E), as well as increased voltage threshold, rheobase, and rheobase charge transfer in MCs of Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 1D and F–H), confirming the hypo-excitable state of MCs in the absence of FMRP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and G.

claim: Loss of FMRP increased rheobase charge transfer in mossy cells.
source: Similarly, we found a decreased number of APs fired (Figure 1D and E), as well as increased voltage threshold, rheobase, and rheobase charge transfer in MCs of Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 1D and F–H), confirming the hypo-excitable state of MCs in the absence of FMRP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and H.

claim: There were no significant changes in AP maximum rise rate, rise time, fall time, duration, peak potential, and amplitude in KO mossy cells.
source: There were no significant changes in AP maximum rise rate, rise time, fall time, duration, peak potential, and amplitude in KO MCs (Figure 1I–N), indicating that the transient Na+ current and fast activating K+ conductances are likely unaffected in MCs of Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I-N.

claim: Transient Na+ current and fast activating K+ conductances are likely unaffected in mossy cells of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: There were no significant changes in AP maximum rise rate, rise time, fall time, duration, peak potential, and amplitude in KO MCs (Figure 1I–N), indicating that the transient Na+ current and fast activating K+ conductances are likely unaffected in MCs of Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of changes in AP parameters shown in Figure 1I-N.

claim: Loss of FMRP did not affect resting membrane potential of mossy cells.
source: We first asked whether this defect was caused by changes in the intrinsic passive membrane properties of MCs by examining the resting membrane potential (RMP), cell capacitance, and input resistance at RMP level, and found all of them to be unaffected in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Loss of FMRP did not affect cell capacitance of mossy cells.
source: We first asked whether this defect was caused by changes in the intrinsic passive membrane properties of MCs by examining the resting membrane potential (RMP), cell capacitance, and input resistance at RMP level, and found all of them to be unaffected in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Loss of FMRP did not affect input resistance at RMP level in mossy cells.
source: We first asked whether this defect was caused by changes in the intrinsic passive membrane properties of MCs by examining the resting membrane potential (RMP), cell capacitance, and input resistance at RMP level, and found all of them to be unaffected in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Input resistance at -45 mV was significantly lower in Fmr1 KO than WT mossy cells.
source: However, since input resistance around the threshold level contributes directly to AP initiation, we examined it again at –45 mV (close to threshold level) using a depolarization step in the pharmacologically isolated MCs (using a combination of blockers against both glutamate and GABA receptors [in μM]: 10 NMDA, 50 APV, 10 MPEP, 5 gabazine and 2 CGP55845) (Deng et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2022), as well as in the presence of 1 μM tetrodotoxin (TTX) and 10 μM CdCl2 to block Na+ and Ca2+ channels, respectively. Under these conditions, the input resistance was significantly lower in Fmr1 KO than WT MCs (Figure 2D and E), suggesting that the reduced input resistance around the threshold potential may be a primary contributor to MC hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Reduced input resistance around the threshold potential may be a primary contributor to MC hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Under these conditions, the input resistance was significantly lower in Fmr1 KO than WT MCs (Figure 2D and E), suggesting that the reduced input resistance around the threshold potential may be a primary contributor to MC hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced input resistance at threshold potential in KO mossy cells.

claim: Kv7 blocker XE991 increased input resistance in all tested mossy cells from both WT and Fmr1 KO mice.
source: We found that the Kv7 blocker XE991 (10 μM) increased input resistance in all tested MCs from both WT and Fmr1 KO (Figure 2E), with a significantly larger effect in KO mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: XE991 had a significantly larger effect on input resistance in KO than WT mossy cells.
source: We found that the Kv7 blocker XE991 (10 μM) increased input resistance in all tested MCs from both WT and Fmr1 KO (Figure 2E), with a significantly larger effect in KO mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: XE991 abolished the difference in input resistance at -45 mV between WT and Fmr1 KO mossy cells.
source: Importantly, XE991 abolished the difference in input resistance at –45 mV between WT and Fmr1 KO cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Kv7 inhibition with XE991 caused a larger shift in the holding current in KO than WT mossy cells.
source: Moreover, Kv7 inhibition with XE991 also caused a larger shift in the holding current in KO than WT MCs (Figure 3A), and a larger membrane depolarization in KO than WT MCs when the membrane potential was initially set at –45 mV (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: XE991 caused a larger membrane depolarization in KO than WT mossy cells when the membrane potential was initially set at -45 mV.
source: Moreover, Kv7 inhibition with XE991 also caused a larger shift in the holding current in KO than WT MCs (Figure 3A), and a larger membrane depolarization in KO than WT MCs when the membrane potential was initially set at –45 mV (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of FMRP increased Kv7 currents in mossy cells.
source: We further observed that loss of FMRP increased Kv7 currents in MCs as measured by a ramp protocol (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Kv7 function is increased in Fmr1 KO mossy cells.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that Kv7 function is increased in Fmr1 KO MCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations showing increased Kv7 activity in KO mossy cells.

claim: There were no changes in expression of KCNQ2 in the whole brain lysate of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: We thus examined whether KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 levels were altered by FMRP loss, but found no changes in expression of either isoform in the whole brain lysate as measured by western blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There were no changes in expression of KCNQ3 in the whole brain lysate of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: We thus examined whether KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 levels were altered by FMRP loss, but found no changes in expression of either isoform in the whole brain lysate as measured by western blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There were no detectable changes in expression of KCNQ2 in dentate gyrus lysate of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: To exclude the possibility that expression variation among brain regions masked KCNQ changes in a particular area, we performed the same experiment on dentate gyrus lysate only. We found no detectable changes in expression of KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There were no detectable changes in expression of KCNQ3 in dentate gyrus lysate of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: To exclude the possibility that expression variation among brain regions masked KCNQ changes in a particular area, we performed the same experiment on dentate gyrus lysate only. We found no detectable changes in expression of KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Hypo-excitability is observed in circuit-isolated mossy cells of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: We first confirmed that hypo-excitability is still observed in these cells when they were isolated from circuit activity using blockers of both glutamate and GABA receptors (as above). We found this to be the case, as evident by increased threshold, rheobase, and rheobase charge transfer (Figure 3E–G), as well as decreased number of APs (Figure 3H) in circuit-isolated MCs of Fmr1 KO comparing to WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: Kv7 blocker XE991 abolished all differences in excitability metrics between WT and KO mossy cells.
source: Importantly, Kv7 blocker XE991 abolished all these differences in excitability metrics between genotypes (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: The hypo-excitability of mossy cells in Fmr1 KO mice has primarily a cell-autonomous origin.
source: Together, these results indicate that the hypo-excitability of MCs in Fmr1 KO mice has primarily a cell-autonomous origin and can be attributed to abnormally elevated Kv7 function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that hypo-excitability persists in pharmacologically isolated mossy cells.

claim: The hypo-excitability of mossy cells in Fmr1 KO mice can be attributed to abnormally elevated Kv7 function.
source: Together, these results indicate that the hypo-excitability of MCs in Fmr1 KO mice has primarily a cell-autonomous origin and can be attributed to abnormally elevated Kv7 function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Kv7 blockade normalizes mossy cell excitability.

claim: The excitatory drive onto mossy cells was increased in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: First, we measured spontaneous and miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs and mEPSCs) and found that the excitatory drive onto MCs was increased, as evident by the elevated number and instantaneous frequency of both sEPSCs and mEPSCs in KO MCs (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), without changes in their amplitudes (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The number and instantaneous frequency of sIPSCs was increased in KO mossy cells.
source: We next examined inhibitory inputs onto MCs and found that the number and instantaneous frequency of spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) was also increased in KO MCs (Figure 4C and D) without changes in amplitude (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: There were no significant differences in mIPSCs in KO mossy cells.
source: However, we did not observe significant differences in miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) in KO MCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: The E/I ratio of inputs onto mossy cells was increased in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Given that the amplitudes of sEPSCs and sIPSCs were indistinguishable between genotypes (Figure 4E and F), we could estimate the E/I ratio simply by using the mean frequency of spontaneous synaptic events (Figure 4G and H) and observed an increased E/I ratio in Fmr1 KO MCs (↑~20%, Figure 4I) which acts in opposition to the intrinsic hypo-excitability observed in MCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The increased E/I ratio in mossy cells acts in opposition to the intrinsic hypo-excitability observed in mossy cells.
source: Given that the amplitudes of sEPSCs and sIPSCs were indistinguishable between genotypes (Figure 4E and F), we could estimate the E/I ratio simply by using the mean frequency of spontaneous synaptic events (Figure 4G and H) and observed an increased E/I ratio in Fmr1 KO MCs (↑~20%, Figure 4I) which acts in opposition to the intrinsic hypo-excitability observed in MCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that increased E/I ratio would tend to increase excitability, which is opposite to the observed hypo-excitability.

claim: Circuit changes likely function as a compensatory mechanism to the intrinsic mossy cell hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Thus, these adaptive circuit changes likely function as a compensatory mechanism to the intrinsic MCs' hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice, similarly to adaptive circuit changes also seen in the cortex (Antoine et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that circuit changes oppose the intrinsic hypo-excitability, and is supported by a citation to similar findings in cortex (Antoine et al., 2019).

claim: Circuit adaptation is insufficient to compensate for MC excitability defects.
source: However, this circuit adaptation is insufficient to compensate for MC excitability defects because we observed overall hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO MCs in the intact circuits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that hypo-excitability persists despite compensatory circuit changes.

claim: The intrinsic excitability of hilar interneurons is not affected significantly in the absence of FMRP.
source: Furthermore, we found that the passive membrane properties (RMP, capacitance and input resistance) and threshold of these interneurons were not significantly different between genotypes and among cell types (thus data were pooled, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E). These results indicate that the intrinsic excitability of hilar interneurons is not affected significantly in the absence of FMRP, suggesting that alterations in synaptic drive onto these cells may play a critical role in determining changes in local inhibition in Fmr1 KOs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: The number and instantaneous frequency of sEPSCs and mEPSCs were markedly decreased in hilar interneurons of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: We found that the number and instantaneous frequency of sEPSCs and mEPSCs were markedly decreased in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G) with no changes in amplitudes (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: The number and instantaneous frequency of sIPSCs were decreased in KO interneurons.
source: Further, the number and instantaneous frequency of sIPSCs were also decreased in KO interneurons (Figure 5C and D) without change in amplitude (Figure 5F), while no significant changes in mIPSCs was observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The E/I ratio of inputs onto hilar interneurons was markedly decreased in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: We then estimated the balance of E/I inputs onto interneurons using the same approach as above for MCs and observed a markedly decreased E/I ratio of inputs onto Fmr1 KO interneurons (↓~60%, Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Mossy cells provide a significant proportion of excitatory drive onto hilar interneurons.
source: In contrast, WIN markedly reduced the normalized frequency of sEPSCs in interneurons of both WT and KO mice (Figure 6B, C, E and F), while it failed to affect the normalized frequency of sEPSC recorded from MCs (Figure 6H and I), suggesting that MCs provide a significant proportion of excitatory drive onto hilar interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, C, E, F, H, and I.

claim: The hypo-excitability of mossy cells in Fmr1 KO mice is a major factor contributing to the reduction of excitatory drive onto hilar interneurons.
source: Together with the observations above, this analysis supports the notion that the hypo-excitability of MCs in Fmr1 KO mice is a major factor contributing to the reduction of excitatory drive onto hilar interneurons, which ultimately results in reduced local inhibition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that mossy cells provide major excitatory drive to interneurons and are hypo-excitable in KO mice.

claim: Circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 channels with XE991 markedly increased sIPSC frequency in the granule cells of Fmr1 KO but not in WT mice.
source: In line with our hypothesis, circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 channels with bath application of XE991 markedly increased sIPSC frequency in the granule cells of Fmr1 KO but not in WT mice (Figure 7C), while having no effect on sEPSC frequency in either genotype (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: XE991 application shifted the E/I balance toward stronger inhibition in the Fmr1 KO, but not in WT mice.
source: As a result, XE991 application shifted the E/I balance toward stronger inhibition in the Fmr1 KO, but not in WT mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Loss of FMRP strongly increased the AP firing in granule cells.
source: To disentangle the direct- and circuit-mediated actions of Kv7 inhibition, we first synaptically isolated granule cells from the circuit using the same pharmacological approach as described above and observed that loss of FMRP strongly increased the AP firing in granule cells (Figure 7E and F, upper panels), as we reported previously (Deng et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and F, and a citation to previous work (Deng et al., 2022).

claim: Intrinsic hyperexcitability of granule cells in Fmr1 KO mice is largely unrelated to Kv7 channels.
source: These results indicate that intrinsic hyperexcitability of granule cells in Fmr1 KO mice is largely unrelated to Kv7 channels. Indeed, we have demonstrated that this intrinsic defect is caused by abnormal extrasynaptic GABAA receptor activity in the absence of FMRP (Deng et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Kv7 blockade does not normalize intrinsic granule cell excitability, and is supported by a citation to previous work (Deng et al., 2022).

claim: Circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 channels with XE991 abolished the difference in the number of APs between genotypes in granule cells with intact circuit.
source: In line with our hypothesis, circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 channels with XE991 abolished the difference in the number of APs between genotypes (Figure 7G and H, lower panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: The circuit action of XE991 resulted in suppressing granule cell excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Specifically, even though the direct action of XE991 on granule cells was to increase excitability in both genotypes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), the circuit action of XE991 resulted in suppressing granule cell excitability in Fmr1 KO mice (↓~6 APs, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), while having minimal effect in WT mice (changes fluctuating around 0, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The primary site of action of XE991 is the mossy cells in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Together with our findings that the interneuron activity is driven in a large part by excitatory input from the MCs, these results indicate that the primary site of action of XE991 is the MCs in Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that XE991 increases inhibitory drive onto granule cells without affecting excitatory drive, and that mossy cells provide major excitatory input to interneurons.

claim: Loss of FMRP significantly decreased the inhibitory component of cPSC and the underlying IPSC in granule cells.
source: In line with our observations above, loss of FMRP significantly decreased the inhibitory component of cPSC and the underlying IPSC (Figure 8D and E, upper panels), while the excitatory component of cPSC was comparable between genotypes (Figure 8C, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: E/I ratio of the inputs onto granule cells was abnormally increased in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: As a result, E/I ratio of the inputs onto granule cells was abnormally increased in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 8F and G, upper panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: A wider excitation window was observed in the granule cells of the KO mice.
source: Moreover, we also observed a wider excitation window (defined as the duration of cPSC excitatory component, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C) in the granule cells of the KO mice (Figure 8H, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 with XE991 significantly increased the inhibitory component of cPSC and underlying IPSC in Fmr1 KO granule cells.
source: In support of our hypothesis, circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 with XE991 significantly increased the inhibitory component of cPSC and underlying IPSC in Fmr1 KO (Figure 8D and E, lower panels), but not in WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Inhibition of Kv7 normalized E/I ratio in the granule cells of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Consequently, inhibition of Kv7 normalized E/I ratio (Figure 8F and G, lower panels), as well as the excitation window in the granule cells of Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 8H, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: Inhibition of Kv7 normalized the excitation window in the granule cells of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Consequently, inhibition of Kv7 normalized E/I ratio (Figure 8F and G, lower panels), as well as the excitation window in the granule cells of Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 8H, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Kv7-dependent hypo-excitability of mossy cells in Fmr1 KO mice is a critical defect in the dentate circuit.
source: These results indicate that Kv7-dependent hypo-excitability of MCs in Fmr1 KO mice is a critical defect in the dentate circuit and that circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 is sufficient to normalize circuit E/I balance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Kv7 inhibition normalizes circuit E/I balance.

claim: Circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 is sufficient to normalize circuit E/I balance.
source: These results indicate that Kv7-dependent hypo-excitability of MCs in Fmr1 KO mice is a critical defect in the dentate circuit and that circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 is sufficient to normalize circuit E/I balance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Kv7 inhibition normalizes E/I ratio and excitation window.

claim: Gamma suppression was much less efficient in the KO than in WT mice.
source: In line with previous studies (Hasselmo et al., 2007; Mircheva et al., 2019), a preceding gamma stimulation suppressed granule cell output in response to theta train in both genotypes (Figure 8I–K, upper panels). However, this gamma suppression was much less efficient in the KO than in WT mice, as evident by the significant higher AP probability in KO mice (Figure 8I–K, upper panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8I-K and citations to previous studies (Hasselmo et al., 2007; Mircheva et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of FMRP causes abnormal dentate information processing, leading to excessive dentate output.
source: Considering that granule cells are the only output neurons in the dentate gyrus and thus integrate all dentate circuit operations, these results indicate that loss of FMRP causes abnormal dentate information processing, leading to excessive dentate output.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing compromised gamma suppression and increased AP probability in KO mice.

claim: Gamma suppression effect was significantly weaker in KO mice.
source: We found that theta stimulation evoked a steady EPSP (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B), and a preceding gamma burst markedly suppressed the EPSP in WT mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B). In line with our results above, this suppression effect was significantly weaker in KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B), suggesting that the compromised dentate inhibitory pathway weakens gamma suppression by enhancing the EPSP summation in the KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Kv7 blocker XE991 reduced the EPSP amplitude in KO mice to the WT level.
source: Indeed, we found that Kv7 blocker XE991 reduced the EPSP amplitude in KO mice to the WT level (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C and D) and, most importantly, normalized gamma suppression of granule cell output during theta activity in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 8J–K, Figure 8—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: XE991 normalized gamma suppression of granule cell output during theta activity in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Indeed, we found that Kv7 blocker XE991 reduced the EPSP amplitude in KO mice to the WT level (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C and D) and, most importantly, normalized gamma suppression of granule cell output during theta activity in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 8J–K, Figure 8—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8J-K and Figure 8—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Mossy cell hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice results in circuit E/I imbalance that compromises the dentate information processing functions.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that MCs' hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice results in circuit E/I imbalance that compromises the dentate information processing functions, and that circuit-based interventions, such as inhibition of Kv7, could be a potential therapeutic strategy to re-normalize the circuit E/I balance and ameliorate dentate dysfunction in FXS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that mossy cell hypo-excitability leads to reduced inhibition and abnormal dentate output.

claim: Circuit-based interventions, such as inhibition of Kv7, could be a potential therapeutic strategy to re-normalize the circuit E/I balance and ameliorate dentate dysfunction in FXS.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that MCs' hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice results in circuit E/I imbalance that compromises the dentate information processing functions, and that circuit-based interventions, such as inhibition of Kv7, could be a potential therapeutic strategy to re-normalize the circuit E/I balance and ameliorate dentate dysfunction in FXS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Kv7 inhibition normalizes circuit E/I balance and dentate output.

claim: Mossy cells have long been considered 'enigmatic' due to their complex and incompletely understood roles in the circuit.
source: These cells have long been considered 'enigmatic' due to their complex and incompletely understood roles in the circuit, yet recently the critical roles of MCs in dentate computations and spatial memory have emerged (Amaral et al., 2007; Berron et al., 2016; Botterill et al., 2021b; Fredes and Shigemoto, 2021; Scharfman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Critical roles of mossy cells in dentate computations and spatial memory have recently emerged.
source: These cells have long been considered 'enigmatic' due to their complex and incompletely understood roles in the circuit, yet recently the critical roles of MCs in dentate computations and spatial memory have emerged (Amaral et al., 2007; Berron et al., 2016; Botterill et al., 2021b; Fredes and Shigemoto, 2021; Scharfman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Amaral et al., 2007; Berron et al., 2016; Botterill et al., 2021b; Fredes and Shigemoto, 2021; Scharfman, 2016).

claim: Mossy cell defects were found to play major roles in epilepsy and many neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Moreover, MC defects were also found to play major roles in epilepsy and many neurodevelopmental disorders (Pelkey et al., 2017; Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018; Noebels et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pelkey et al., 2017; Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018; Noebels et al., 2012).

claim: Mossy cell hypo-excitability was observed both in the synaptically isolated mossy cells and with the intact circuit.
source: Since MC hypo-excitability was observed both in the synaptically isolated MCs and with the intact circuit, this defect has a cell-autonomous origin and the adaptive circuit changes were insufficient to compensate for it.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing hypo-excitability in both isolated and circuit-intact conditions.

claim: FMRP is known to regulate activity of several K+ channels, including Slack, BK, SK, and Kv1.2 via protein-protein interactions.
source: In addition to translational regulation, FMRP is also known to regulate activity of several K+ channels, including Slack, BK, SK, and Kv1.2 via protein–protein interactions (Deng and Klyachko, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Deng and Klyachko, 2021).

claim: In all cases where FMRP regulates K+ channels via protein-protein interactions, FMRP loss decreases rather than increases K+ channel activity.
source: However, in all of these cases, FMRP loss decreases rather than increases K+ channel activity, making loss of protein–protein interactions an unlikely mechanism to explain increased Kv7 function.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about FMRP's effects on K+ channels.

claim: Activation of PKC suppresses Kv7 function.
source: For example, activation of PKC suppresses Kv7 function (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Haick et al., 2017) and PKCε expression was found to be reduced in hippocampus of Fmr1 KO mice (Marsillo et al., 2021), supporting a possibility that the increased Kv7 function in KO MCs may be associated with abnormal PKC signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Haick et al., 2017).

claim: PKCε expression was found to be reduced in hippocampus of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: For example, activation of PKC suppresses Kv7 function (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Haick et al., 2017) and PKCε expression was found to be reduced in hippocampus of Fmr1 KO mice (Marsillo et al., 2021), supporting a possibility that the increased Kv7 function in KO MCs may be associated with abnormal PKC signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Marsillo et al., 2021).

claim: The increased Kv7 function in KO mossy cells may be associated with abnormal PKC signaling.
source: For example, activation of PKC suppresses Kv7 function (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Haick et al., 2017) and PKCε expression was found to be reduced in hippocampus of Fmr1 KO mice (Marsillo et al., 2021), supporting a possibility that the increased Kv7 function in KO MCs may be associated with abnormal PKC signaling.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that PKC suppresses Kv7 and PKCε is reduced in KO mice.

claim: The increase in excitatory drive onto mossy cells likely reflects the hyper-excitable state of granule cells.
source: We note that this increase in excitatory drive cannot explain the MCs' hypo-excitability; rather these results likely reflect the hyper-excitable state of granule cells (Deng et al., 2022), which provide the majority of excitatory drive onto MCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that granule cells are hyper-excitable and provide major excitatory input to mossy cells, supported by a citation (Deng et al., 2022).

claim: Granule cells provide the majority of excitatory drive onto mossy cells.
source: We note that this increase in excitatory drive cannot explain the MCs' hypo-excitability; rather these results likely reflect the hyper-excitable state of granule cells (Deng et al., 2022), which provide the majority of excitatory drive onto MCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about dentate circuit connectivity.

claim: Stellate cells have normal excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: In the Fmr1 KO mice, stellate cells have normal excitability (Deng and Klyachko, 2016); the granule cells are hyper-excitable (Deng et al., 2022), while MCs are hypo-excitable.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Deng and Klyachko, 2016).

claim: Granule cells are hyper-excitable in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: In the Fmr1 KO mice, stellate cells have normal excitability (Deng and Klyachko, 2016); the granule cells are hyper-excitable (Deng et al., 2022), while MCs are hypo-excitable.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Deng et al., 2022).

claim: Granule cell- and PP-derived EPSCs comprise a limited portion of excitatory drive onto hilar interneurons in both genotypes.
source: We observed that DCG-IV had little effect on the normalized frequency of sEPSCs recorded in interneurons in both genotypes (Figure 6A, C, D and F), indicating that granule cell- and PP-derived EPSCs comprise a limited portion of excitatory drive onto hilar interneurons in both genotypes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that DCG-IV had little effect on sEPSC frequency in interneurons.

claim: Mossy cells relay and expand granule cell-derived excitatory drive onto interneurons.
source: In their control of inhibition, the MCs relay and expand granule cell-derived excitatory drive onto interneurons, which then convert this drive into stronger feedback inhibition onto granule cells (Botterill et al., 2021a; Hashimotodani et al., 2017; Houser et al., 2021; Yeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Botterill et al., 2021a; Hashimotodani et al., 2017; Houser et al., 2021; Yeh et al., 2018).

claim: During network activity, short-term plasticity actively modulates outputs from both excitatory and inhibitory synapses to dynamically fine-tune the E/I drives.
source: Notably, the resulting E/I balance driving granule cell output is not static; rather, during network activity, short-term plasticity actively modulates outputs from both excitatory and inhibitory synapses to dynamically fine-tune the E/I drives and optimize neural computations (Bartley and Dobrunz, 2015; Bhatia et al., 2019; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bartley and Dobrunz, 2015; Bhatia et al., 2019; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018).

claim: Granule cells normally fire sparsely during information processing.
source: Given that granule cells normally fire sparsely during information processing, this increased AP output in granule cells is reminiscent of abnormal CA3-to-CA1 information transmission in the Fmr1 KO mice, in which a large amount of ''noise' that is normally filtered out during synaptic processing is being transmitted indiscriminately due to FMRP loss (Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about granule cell firing patterns.

claim: FMRP plays a crucial role in synaptogenesis and synaptic refinement.
source: Indeed, FMRP plays a crucial role in synaptogenesis and synaptic refinement (Booker et al., 2019; Doll and Broadie, 2014; Kennedy et al., 2020; Sears and Broadie, 2017), and loss of FMRP is well known to cause changes in synaptic connectivity (Gibson et al., 2008; Kennedy et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Tessier and Broadie, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Booker et al., 2019; Doll and Broadie, 2014; Kennedy et al., 2020; Sears and Broadie, 2017).

claim: Loss of FMRP is well known to cause changes in synaptic connectivity.
source: Indeed, FMRP plays a crucial role in synaptogenesis and synaptic refinement (Booker et al., 2019; Doll and Broadie, 2014; Kennedy et al., 2020; Sears and Broadie, 2017), and loss of FMRP is well known to cause changes in synaptic connectivity (Gibson et al., 2008; Kennedy et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Tessier and Broadie, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gibson et al., 2008; Kennedy et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Tessier and Broadie, 2009).

claim: Many of the cellular and synaptic changes in the Fmr1 KO mice are antagonistic and mitigating circuit dysfunction, and thus compensate for the primary defects.
source: Indeed, many of the cellular and synaptic changes in the Fmr1 KO mice are antagonistic and mitigating circuit dysfunction, and thus compensate for the primary defects (Domanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Domanski et al., 2019).

claim: E/I balance is dynamically tuned to rapidly adjust during circuit computations.
source: Indeed, as discussed above, E/I balance is dynamically tuned to rapidly adjust during circuit computations (Bartley and Dobrunz, 2015; Bhatia et al., 2019; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018), which is thought to represent a fundamental mechanism underlying efficient neural coding (Zhou and Yu, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bartley and Dobrunz, 2015; Bhatia et al., 2019; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018).

claim: Dynamic E/I balance is thought to represent a fundamental mechanism underlying efficient neural coding.
source: Indeed, as discussed above, E/I balance is dynamically tuned to rapidly adjust during circuit computations (Bartley and Dobrunz, 2015; Bhatia et al., 2019; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018), which is thought to represent a fundamental mechanism underlying efficient neural coding (Zhou and Yu, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Zhou and Yu, 2018).

claim: Theta-gamma oscillation coupling plays a critical role in dentate information processing.
source: Considering that the theta–gamma oscillation coupling plays a critical role in dentate information processing (Bott et al., 2016; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Mizuseki et al., 2009; Neves et al., 2022; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014), our findings indicate that MC-driven E/I imbalance is a critical defect contributing to dentate dysfunction in FXS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bott et al., 2016; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Mizuseki et al., 2009; Neves et al., 2022; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014).

claim: Mossy cells project axons both ipsi- and contralaterally along the longitudinal axis of the dentate gyrus.
source: Moreover, by projecting axons both ipsi- and contralaterally along the longitudinal axis of the dentate gyrus, MCs are uniquely positioned to influence dentate activity widely across lamellae (Jinde et al., 2013; Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jinde et al., 2013; Scharfman, 2016; Scharfman, 2018).

claim: Mossy cell hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice is a core defect in the dysregulation of circuit E/I dynamics and information processing.
source: This wide-reaching control of dentate activity makes MC hypo-excitability in Fmr1 KO mice a core defect in the dysregulation of circuit E/I dynamics and information processing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mossy cells have wide-reaching influence on dentate activity and their hypo-excitability leads to circuit dysfunction.

claim: Circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 was sufficient to re-normalize E/I balance in the dentate circuit despite the irreconcilable hypo-excitable state of mossy cells and hyper-excitable state of granule cells in the Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Most critical discovery in this regard is our finding that circuit-wide inhibition of Kv7 was sufficient to re-normalize E/I balance in the dentate circuit despite the irreconcilable hypo-excitable state of MCs and hyper-excitable state of granule cells in the Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Kv7 inhibition normalizes E/I balance and circuit function.

claim: XE991 corrected mossy cell hypo-excitability via direct effect on Kv7 channels in mossy cells.
source: Specifically, XE991 corrected MC hypo-excitability via direct effect on Kv7 channels in MCs and normalized granule cell excitability through dentate three-synapse feedback pathway in Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that XE991 increases mossy cell excitability.

claim: XE991 normalized granule cell excitability through dentate three-synapse feedback pathway in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Specifically, XE991 corrected MC hypo-excitability via direct effect on Kv7 channels in MCs and normalized granule cell excitability through dentate three-synapse feedback pathway in Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that XE991 increases inhibitory drive onto granule cells and normalizes their excitability.

claim: Inhibition of Kv7 channels was sufficient to restore the dentate output during the physiologically relevant theta-gamma coupling activity in KO mice.
source: Moreover, inhibition of Kv7 channels was also sufficient to restore the dentate output during the physiologically relevant theta–gamma coupling activity in KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that XE991 normalizes gamma suppression of dentate output.

claim: The excessive Kv7 function is present selectively in mossy cells of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: This effect arises because the excessive Kv7 function is present selectively in MCs of Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased Kv7 function specifically in mossy cells.

claim: Inhibition of Kv7 had a stronger effect on enhancing MC-dependent feedback inhibition onto granule cells than directly increasing granule cell excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: As a result, inhibition of Kv7 had a stronger effect on enhancing MC-dependent feedback inhibition onto granule cells than directly increasing granule cell excitability in Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the net effect of XE991 is to suppress granule cell excitability in KO mice.

claim: Circuit-based interventions can represent a potential therapeutic strategy to correct dentate dysfunction in FXS.
source: Thus, circuit-based interventions can represent a potential therapeutic strategy to correct dentate dysfunction in this disorder.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the experimental data showing that circuit-wide Kv7 inhibition normalizes dentate function in vitro.

claim: The power of theta-gamma oscillations is particularly high in the dentate gyrus.
source: The power of theta–gamma oscillations is particularly high in the dentate gyrus (Csicsvari et al., 2003) and plays a critical role in many dentate functions, such as pattern separation (Leutgeb et al., 2007), information coding (Mizuseki et al., 2009; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014), and thus learning/memory (Bott et al., 2016; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Neves et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Csicsvari et al., 2003).

claim: Theta-gamma oscillations play a critical role in pattern separation.
source: The power of theta–gamma oscillations is particularly high in the dentate gyrus (Csicsvari et al., 2003) and plays a critical role in many dentate functions, such as pattern separation (Leutgeb et al., 2007), information coding (Mizuseki et al., 2009; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014), and thus learning/memory (Bott et al., 2016; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Neves et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Leutgeb et al., 2007).

source: The power of theta–gamma oscillations is particularly high in the dentate gyrus (Csicsvari et al., 2003) and plays a critical role in many dentate functions, such as pattern separation (Leutgeb et al., 2007), information coding (Mizuseki et al., 2009; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014), and thus learning/memory (Bott et al., 2016; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Neves et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mizuseki et al., 2009; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014).

claim: Theta-gamma oscillations play a critical role in learning and memory.
source: The power of theta–gamma oscillations is particularly high in the dentate gyrus (Csicsvari et al., 2003) and plays a critical role in many dentate functions, such as pattern separation (Leutgeb et al., 2007), information coding (Mizuseki et al., 2009; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014), and thus learning/memory (Bott et al., 2016; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Neves et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bott et al., 2016; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Neves et al., 2022).

claim: The dentate GABAergic system plays a critical role in gamma suppression of granule cell output.
source: The dentate GABAergic system plays a critical role in the above gamma suppression of granule cell output (Mircheva et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mircheva et al., 2019).

claim: The compromised dentate inhibitory pathway in the Fmr1 KO mice weakens gamma suppression by enhancing the EPSP summation in granule cells.
source: Based on our findings, we hypothesized that the compromised dentate inhibitory pathway in the Fmr1 KO mice weakens gamma suppression by enhancing the EPSP summation in granule cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced inhibition and enhanced EPSP summation in KO mice.
